The peripheral blood smear is notable for large, often oval RBCs with increased mean corpuscular volume.
The mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of HS erythrocytes is low normal or even slightly decreased, and the mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration (MCHC) is usually increased (>35 g/dL).
HPP is characterized by extreme microcytosis (mean corpuscular volume, 50- 65 fL/cell), extraordinary variation in cell size and shape, and microspherocytosis with occasional elliptocytosis.

qs.q: An exclusively breastfed 4-month-old infant presents with severe pallor, irritability, and poor weight gain. Laboratory tests reveal a hemoglobin of 6 g/dL with a normal mean corpuscular volume and normal reticulocyte count. Which diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?
o: Severe iron deficiency anemia from poor maternal stores
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia triggered by viral illness
G6PD deficiency presenting with acute hemolytic crisis
Beta-thalassemia major manifesting early in infancy
qs.e: Diamond-Blackfan anemia typically presents in early infancy with severe normocytic anemia and a selective deficiency of red cell precursors.

qs.q: A 72-year-old woman is scheduled for elective total hip replacement in 4 weeks. Her preoperative laboratory results show a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, serum ferritin of 12 ng/mL, and mean corpuscular volume of 74 fL. Which management strategy is most appropriate prior to surgery?
o: Give oral iron and keep the surgery date unchanged
Give two units of packed red cells before the scheduled operation
Go ahead with surgery as planned and depend on intra‑operative cell salvage
Administer IV iron and postpone surgery until hemoglobin rises
qs.e: Intravenous iron corrects iron-deficiency anemia preoperatively and allows clinical optimization before elective major joint surgery associated with substantial blood loss. Oral iron takes several weeks to months to replenish stores and is insufficient to optimize hemoglobin within a short timeframe.

qs.q: A 65-year-old man who underwent total gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma two years ago presents with progressive fatigue, paresthesias in both feet, and mild memory impairment. Laboratory evaluation reveals a mean corpuscular volume of 108 fL. Deficiency of which nutrient is responsible for these clinical manifestations?
qs.e: Total gastrectomy removes parietal cells that produce intrinsic factor, leading to vitamin B12 malabsorption manifested as macrocytic anemia and peripheral neuropathy. Folate deficiency also causes macrocytic anemia but does not produce neurological deficits.

qs.q: In the classification of anaemia based on morphological characteristics using the mean corpuscular volume (MCV), which of the following conditions is classified under the microcytic category (MCV <80 fL)?
o: Megaloblastic anaemia due to B12 deficiency
qs.e: Iron deficiency anaemia, thalassaemia, and anaemia of chronic disease are classic examples of microcytic anaemia where the MCV falls below 80 fL. Conversely, B12 and folate deficiencies produce macrocytic anaemia with an MCV above 100 fL.
qs.s: Year 3: Haematology and Blood Transfusion Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents with mild fatigue. Her haemoglobin is 10.5 g/dL with a normal mean corpuscular volume. Which physiological process accounts for this finding?
o: Placental transfer causing absolute maternal iron depletion
Plasma volume expansion exceeding red cell mass increase
Gestational alloimmune destruction of circulating erythrocytes
qs.e: During normal pregnancy, plasma volume increases to a greater extent than red cell mass, leading to a physiological dilutional anaemia. In contrast, absolute iron deficiency results in microcytosis rather than normal red cell indices.
qs.s: Haematology & Blood Transfusion Pathology: MDS, Stem Cell Transplant: MCQs

qs.q: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for a persistent microcytic anemia. Laboratory workup reveals low hemoglobin and low mean corpuscular volume. Which additional red cell parameter best distinguishes iron deficiency anemia from beta-thalassemia trait?
qs.e: Iron deficiency anemia typically presents with an elevated red cell distribution width reflecting anisocytosis, whereas beta-thalassemia minor usually shows a normal red cell distribution width. Both conditions feature microcytic red blood cells.

es.q: List and explain the major categories of anaemia based on mean corpuscular volume (MCV).
es.m:
- **Normocytic (MCV 80–100 fL)** – most commonly due to anaemia of chronic disease; may also be early iron deficiency or combined deficiencies.
- **Microcytic (MCV < 80 fL)** – includes iron‑deficiency anaemia (high RDW), thalassaemia minor (normal RDW), sideroblastic anaemia, and metal poisoning.
- **Macrocytic (MCV > 100 fL)** – MCV > 110 fL usually folate or cobalamin deficiency; MCV 100–110 fL requires evaluation for other causes such as alcoholism, liver disease, or drug effects.
- **Clinical relevance** – MCV directs the subsequent work‑up (iron studies for microcytic, B12/folate for macrocytic, and evaluation for chronic disease for normocytic).

ai.title: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: MCV measures the average size of red blood cells and guides the classification of anaemia. Interpreting MCV helps clinicians narrow differential diagnoses, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: MCV is the calculated average volume of a single erythrocyte, expressed in femtolitres (fL). It is derived from the complete blood count (CBC) using the formula: MCV = (Hematocrit ÷ RBC count) × 10.
b: Normal adult range: 80–100 fL (adjust for age and altitude).
Microcytosis: <80 fL; Macrocytosis: >100 fL.

sections.p: MCV itself is not staged, but it directs the severity assessment of the underlying anaemia.
b: Mild anaemia: Hb ≥ 11 g/dL; Moderate: 8–10.9 g/dL; Severe: <8 g/dL.

sections.p: Classify by cell size; then consider epidemiology of the region.
b: Microcytic: iron‑deficiency (chronic malaria, hookworm, menstrual loss), thalassaemia trait, chronic disease, sideroblastic anaemia.

Macrocytic: folate deficiency (poor diet, malabsorption), vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, malabsorption, strict vegetarianism), alcohol excess, drug‑induced (e.g., zidovudine, antiretrovirals), haemolysis with reticulocytosis.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with fatigue, dyspnoea on exertion, pallor, tachycardia, or, in severe cases, heart failure.
b: Microcytic anaemia often shows spoon‑shaped cells on smear.
Macrocytic anaemia may show oval macro‑ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

t.b: What is the overall anaemia pattern? – Confirms low Hb and gives MCV to categorise anaemia.
What does cell morphology show? – Microcytosis with hypochromia suggests iron deficiency; macro‑ovalocytes suggest folate/B12 deficiency.
Is iron deficiency present? – Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; normal/high ferritin suggests other causes.
Is a vitamin deficiency causing macrocytosis? – Low folate or B12 confirms macrocytic anaemia.
Is the marrow responding? – High retic in haemolysis or recent blood loss; low retic in production problems.
Is a haemoglobinopathy present? – Detects thalassaemia or sickle‑cell disease.

sections.p: Severe anaemia can precipitate cardiac decompensation, especially in patients with pre‑existing heart disease or pregnancy.
b: Chest pain, syncope, or new‑onset heart failure.
Rapidly falling Hb (<7 g/dL) in a previously stable patient.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide supportive therapy while monitoring for complications.
b: Iron deficiency: oral ferrous sulfate (if tolerated) or parenteral iron when malabsorption or severe loss.
Avoid folate supplementation before confirming B12 deficiency to prevent masking neurologic damage.
In haemolytic or sickle‑cell crises, give transfusion if Hb < 7 g/dL or symptomatic.
If CBC or iron studies unavailable, treat empirically for iron deficiency in patients with chronic malaria or hookworm and microcytosis.

sections.p: Re‑check CBC and MCV after 4–6 weeks of therapy to confirm response. Prevent recurrence by addressing dietary gaps and parasitic infections.
b: Repeat iron studies after 2 months of therapy.
Deworming programmes and malaria prophylaxis in endemic areas.
Nutrition education focusing on leafy greens, legumes, and fortified grains.

sections.p: Mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH) and mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration (MCHC) are related indices but describe haemoglobin content, not cell size.
b: Low MCHC suggests hypochromic anaemia; normal MCHC with low MCV points to iron deficiency.

sections.p: Certain conditions alter MCV without true size change.
b: Reticulocytosis raises MCV because reticulocytes are larger.
Cold agglutinins can cause spuriously high MCV.
Severe dehydration concentrates blood, falsely lowering MCV.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in Hb with chest pain or syncope
New‑onset heart failure signs in an anaemic patient
Neurologic symptoms (paresthesia, gait disturbance) suggesting B12 deficiency

faq.q: Why can iron deficiency cause a low MCV?
faq.a: Insufficient iron limits haemoglobin synthesis, producing smaller, hypochromic red cells.

faq.q: Can macrocytosis occur with normal B12 and folate?
faq.a: Yes – alcohol excess, liver disease, and certain drugs (e.g., zidovudine) enlarge red cells without vitamin deficiency.

faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot measure MCV?
faq.a: Rely on peripheral smear morphology and clinical context; treat empirically for the most likely cause.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer with chronic malaria presents with Hb 9 g/dL and MCV 72 fL. What is the next diagnostic step? — Order serum ferritin and stool for occult blood; low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, common after repeated malaria‑induced haemolysis.

A patient on zidovudine for HIV has Hb 11 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, and no neurologic signs. How should you manage the anaemia? — Continue antiretroviral therapy, add folic acid, and monitor; avoid switching drugs unless severe.

You receive a CBC showing MCV 85 fL but the smear shows many oval macro‑ovalocytes. What does this discrepancy indicate? — Reticulocytosis or mixed anaemia; repeat CBC after addressing the underlying cause.
A child with sickle‑cell disease has Hb 7 g/dL, MCV 78 fL. What is the most urgent intervention? — Transfuse packed red cells if symptomatic or if Hb <7 g/dL with signs of cardiac strain.

A 60‑year‑old man with chronic kidney disease has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 95 fL, and normal iron studies. What is the likely cause of his anaemia? — Anaemia of chronic disease; treat with erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents if indicated.
Why must you avoid giving folic acid before confirming B12 deficiency? — Folate can correct the haematologic picture while neurologic damage from B12 deficiency progresses unnoticed.
